title: The Soul's Cry and the Nature of Faith
english: It says, to the child of the Lord, David. A conclusion to be taken from these things is victory over all enemies; for on account of this both wars and everything contributing to the excellence of a king exist. And it is rightly said that it is not the other things, but this itself, that triumphs. For since victory exists, it is not necessary to give thanks to anyone else but to God who granted it. For it is said to him by Ezra: 'From you is the victory.'

David refers the song to the Lord, as his child and servant, having wisely and faithfully expressed all the words of thanksgiving on that day (that is, in that light), in which all the enemies and Saul the king of Israel were overthrown, and David was rescued unharmed from them. And these things are [said] as regarding the history.

But since it seems to many of the faithful that the song is present from the face of the Savior, it must be said that the triumphal hymn refers to the resurrection from the dead, his being rescued from all the guarding nations and the empty peoples who studied [to destroy him], but also from the kings who stood against him and the rulers gathered against him. And you say that he was rescued also from the hand of Saul, who was then ruling the Jews, in a certain way; for it was not an inaccurate representation of their manner, being wrathful and having with them an evil spirit, saying they did not have a god for a king; for how could they not be about to deny God, to be ruled by some base person? (Ps 17:5b,6).

'Streams of iniquity' were called, as another says, and because of entering into iniquity those who do not bravely stand against the trials. And if the preceding words concern the death that follows those who sin, and the harmony having with it slavery, then the pains of death and slavery are the sins that exist toward death. In accordance with this understanding, you will say 'streams of iniquity' [referring to] the currents of wickedness, and 'snares of death' [referring to] those which practically constitute sins toward death.

According to the previous explanation, the present passages fit the economy of the Lord according to the flesh. For 'My soul is greatly troubled, and my soul is very sorrowful near death' (Ps 17:7) possesses much intimacy with the Now.

Prayer has much boldness from a pure conscience, since to call upon the Lord is not a mere report, but to cry out to God. Lest it be not in agreement with us that God is the Father and Jesus Christ is Lord. We shall call God the Father and the Son Lord, unless both are said of the same one as Father and Son of God and Lord, being through the same divinity and lordship. How then, having said 'He heard my voice from His holy temple?' (Ps 17:7) It is said metaphorically that his cry enters into the ears of God. To this, one says: that having heard God, the one who prayed will become out of the distress, believing that, having cried again to God, he receives him into the ears and before him the upward-sent cry. Another saying: the one who perceived through the calling from His holy temple that the Paraclete had breathed upon him, is emboldened that he will find the outcome of those things for which he cried, the cry being sent up from a pure disposition into the ears of God and before Him.

These oracles remove from the deceived those having faith like a grain of mustard seed (Ps 17:8b); for if Paul says that faith as a grain of mustard seed removes [them]. Among these was also the spirit of moon-sickness about which the Savior says: 'If you have faith like a grain of mustard seed, you say to this mountain, Move from here to there' (Ps 17:9).
